title: Given an array of positive numbers and a window size k, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of exactly k elements. (GeeksforGeeks: Max Sum Subarray of size K)
shortTitle: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K (Fixed-Size Sliding Window)

s1_definition.profdef: The maximum-sum-subarray-of-size-k problem uses a fixed-size sliding window. You compute the sum of the first k elements, then slide the window forward one position at a time by adding the incoming element and subtracting the outgoing element, tracking the maximum sum seen. This reuses the previous sum rather than recomputing, giving linear time and constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants the best k-day stretch of daily deposits, the window of exactly k consecutive days whose total is highest. Instead of re-adding every k-day block from scratch, he keeps a running total for the current window, and each time he slides to the next day he adds the new day's deposit on the right and drops the oldest day's deposit on the left. He watches the running total and remembers the largest it ever reaches.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sum the first window once, then slide by adding the new element and subtracting the old one, tracking the max.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The maximum-sum-subarray-of-size-k problem uses a fixed-size sliding window. You compute the sum of the first k elements, then slide the window forward one position at a time by adding the incoming element and subtracting the outgoing element, tracking the maximum sum seen. This reuses the previous sum rather than recomputing, giving linear time and constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants the best k-day stretch of daily deposits, the window of exactly k consecutive days whose total is highest. Instead of re-adding every k-day block from scratch, he keeps a running total for the current window, and each time he slides to the next day he adds the new day's deposit on the right and drops the oldest day's deposit on the left. He watches the running total and remembers the largest it ever reaches.

**One line to remember:** Sum the first window once, then slide by adding the new element and subtracting the old one, tracking the max.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach computes the sum of every possible window of size k independently, which repeats a lot of addition and costs k times n work. The sliding window exploits the fact that consecutive windows overlap in all but two elements, so we can update the sum in constant time per slide.

We first add up the first k elements to get the initial window sum and set it as the current maximum. Then we slide: for each new right edge from index k to the end, we add the element entering on the right and subtract the element leaving on the left, which keeps the running sum correct for the new window. After each slide we compare the running sum to the maximum and update the maximum if the new sum is larger. When we reach the end, the maximum holds the answer.

A finance usage example: suppose daily deposits are `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]` and k is 3. The first window `[3, 1, 4]` sums to 8, which becomes the max. Sliding to `[1, 4, 1]` we add 1 and subtract 3, giving 6. Sliding to `[4, 1, 5]` we add 5 and subtract 1, giving 10, which is larger, so the max becomes 10. The best three-day stretch totals 10.

The senior-level nuance: the sliding window turns a k-times-n brute force into a clean linear scan, which matters when both the array and k are large. An edge case is when k is larger than the array length, in which case no valid window exists and the method should signal that clearly. This fixed-size window differs from the variable-size window used in minimum-length or longest-substring problems, where the window grows and shrinks based on a condition; here the window size is constant, which keeps the logic especially simple.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's analytics team reviews a customer's daily deposit history and wants to highlight the single best stretch of exactly k consecutive days, the window with the highest total inflow, for a marketing insight. Recomputing every k-day block independently is wasteful over long histories.

Problem 2 — The computation runs frequently across many customers, so it must be efficient and use minimal memory, which the sliding window with a reusable running sum provides.

The code defines a `DepositWindowAnalyzer` class with a `maxWindowSum` method implementing the fixed-size sliding window. A runnable demo seeds a deposit history and a window size and logs the maximum window total.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the deposits `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]` and window size k equal to 3.

Step 1: The analyzer sums the first three deposits, 3 plus 1 plus 4, giving a window sum of 8. This becomes the initial maximum.

Step 2: It slides the window to the right edge at index 3. It adds the entering deposit 1 and subtracts the leaving deposit 3, so the window sum becomes 8 plus 1 minus 3, equal to 6. Since 6 is not larger than 8, the maximum stays at 8.

Step 3: It slides to the right edge at index 4. It adds the entering deposit 5 and subtracts the leaving deposit 1 (the one at index 1), so the window sum becomes 6 plus 5 minus 1, equal to 10. Since 10 is larger than 8, the maximum updates to 10.

Step 4: The right edge has reached the end of the array, so the sliding stops. The windows considered were `[3,1,4]` summing to 8, `[1,4,1]` summing to 6, and `[4,1,5]` summing to 10.

Step 5: The method returns the maximum, 10, which corresponds to the best three-day deposit stretch at the end of the history.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 7:25:00 PM com.bank.analytics.DepositWindowDemo main
INFO: Deposits: [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], k=3
INFO: Max sum of any 3-day window = 10
INFO: Best 3-day deposit total = 10
```

```

    ▼
  slide → [1,4,1]: +1 -3 → 6   max=8
  slide → [4,1,5]: +5 -1 → 10  max=10
    ▼
  max window sum = 10
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum-sum-subarray-of-size-k problem is the textbook fixed-size sliding window, and the whole trick is to avoid recomputing overlapping work. A brute-force solution computes the sum of every window of size k from scratch, which repeats most of the additions and costs k times n, but consecutive windows overlap in all but two elements, so I can update the running sum in constant time per slide.

I first add up the initial window of the first k elements and treat that as both my running sum and my current maximum. Then I slide the window forward one position at a time: at each step I add the element entering on the right and subtract the element leaving on the left, which keeps the running sum exactly correct for the new window without touching the middle elements. After each slide I compare the running sum to the maximum and keep the larger. When the window reaches the end of the array, the maximum holds the answer, and the whole scan is linear time with constant extra space.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the analytics team. We reviewed a customer's daily deposit history and wanted to highlight the single best stretch of exactly k consecutive days, the window with the highest total inflow, for a marketing insight. Because we ran this frequently across many customers over long histories, the efficient sliding window with a reusable running sum kept the computation fast and memory-light.

The senior-level point I make is to distinguish this fixed-size window from the variable-size window used in other problems. Here the window size never changes, so the logic is simply add-one-subtract-one per slide; in problems like smallest subarray with a given sum or longest substring with a condition, the window grows and shrinks dynamically based on a constraint, which is a different pattern. I also call out the edge case where k exceeds the array length, in which case there is no valid window and the method should fail clearly rather than silently returning a wrong value. Being precise about which flavor of sliding window a problem needs is what shows I understand the family rather than memorizing one instance.
